To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) when a group is subject to strong negative reputational externalitites, it cannot escape a low-skill trap, regardless of expectations, and (b) the more a group's reputation is hurt by its low average skill, the more it should be helped by egalitarian policies.

1) the evolution of a group's collective reputation is determined by its members' average skill and the strength of reputational externality; 2) a bad collective reputation can trap a group into low skill investment; 3) a bad reputation cannot be escaped when the group is strongly affected negatively by reputational externalities; and 4) egalitarian policies can be effective when they reduce the strength of negative reputational externalites.

(1) a bad reputation can become a self-fulfillingly bad equilibrium in the sense that the group is unable to escape a low skill trap, even if expectations are not formed in a self-ful-filling manner; and (2) the more the group's reputation affects the productivity of group members, the more difficult it is for the group to escape from the low skill trap, and the less effective are egalitarian policies.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the evolution of stereotypes.
the evolution of stereotypes and the dynamics of statistical discrimination.
the role of reputation in shaping the dynamics of statistical discrimination.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
a group's collective reputation can be a source of both fragility and intractability.
a bad equilibrium can only be escaped by a group when the group is not too large, and when it is able to overcome negative reputational externalitie.

a dynamic version of the Coate-Loury model, in which the group is strongly affected, is a useful framework to study the evolution of group stereotypes, the dynamics of statistical discrimination, and the effectiveness of egalitarian policies.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
a bad equilibrium in a statistical discrimination model is fragile only if it is not strongly affected by negative reputation effects.
the more a group is affected by negative reputations, the more difficult it is for the group to escape the bad equilibrium, and the less likely that egalitarian policies can help the group to escape.
, if the group is strongly affected and has a high degree of homogeneity, then egalitarian policies are not likely to be successful.
The main takeaway from our work is that
policies aimed at improving the reputation of disadvantaged groups may not be as effective as is commonly believed, because of negative reputational externalites.
the most efficient policy to break a low skill equilibrium is a policy that reduces the negative reputational external effects on the group's members.
, in a dynamic model, the effects of egalitarian policies on the evolution of stereotypes are ambiguous.
